title.en: Diarmuid Climbs the Rock and Dives the Enchanter's Well
title.zh: 迪爾穆德攀岩與躍入巫師之井

region.en: Grey cliff over the western sea, Corca Duibhne (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 科爾卡·迪夫尼西海外灰色絕壁（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn under bonds follows the Gilla Decair over sea, and thirteen of the Fianna hang from the mistletoe-cliff of a great grey rock. Fergus shames Diarmuid — reared by Manannan the Powerful and Angus Og — and he rises on Manannan's staves of power to the overhanging rock. There the Enchanter of the thicket fights him day after day at the enchanted well until both fall in; below lies a flowery plain, a royal city, and a house of healing where Diarmuid is made sound again.
summary.zh: 芬恩受誓追隨劣僕出海；菲亞納十三人懸於灰色巨岩之上。費爾古斯以「受教於大能瑪那南與安古斯·奧格」羞激迪爾穆德，他遂持瑪那南之力杖躍上懸岩。岩後密林中，巫師在魔井邊與他日復一日搏鬥，直至二人同墜井底；井底之下是繁花平原與王城，迪爾穆德在療傷之屋重獲健全。

sensitivity.note: The tree-horn-well sequence is the classic entry to the otherworld (the enchanted drink compels the duel — cf. the fixed well-and-keeper motif of immram literature). Manannan's staves of power are Diarmuid's inherited divine gifts. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Finn and the Fianna rose up then, and they followed the Gilla Decair over every bald hill, and through every valley and every river, on to pleasant Slieve Luachra, into the borders of Corca Duibhne; and the big man, that was up on the horse then along with Conan and the rest, faced towards the deep sea, and Liagan Luath of Luachar took hold of the horse's tail with his two hands, and away with him over the sea, and Liagan along with him, holding on to his tail. "The Tuatha de Danaan left as a gift to the children of the Gael, that whoever might have to leave Ireland for a while had but to go to Beinn Edair, and however many would go along with him, they would find a ship that would hold them all." And Feradach, the Very Brave, son of the King of the Eastern World, struck three blows on his sling-stick with his carpenter's axe, and the whole of the bay and of the harbour was filled with ships and with fast boats.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: They went on over the restless hills of the great sea for three days and three nights, and saw a great rough grey cliff with a high round rock on its edge, having sides more slippery than an eel's back, and they found the track of the Hard Servant as far as to the foot of the rock. "It is no brave thing you are doing, Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, to hold back like this, for it was with Manannan the Powerful, son of Lir, you were reared and got your learning, in the Land of Promise and in the coasts of the harbours, and with Angus Og, the Dagda's son." Diarmuid's face reddened when he heard those words, and he took hold of Manannan's staves of power that were with him, and he rose on the staves and gave a leap, and got a standing-place for his two feet on the overhanging rock.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: He was not gone far when he saw a great tree with many twigs and branches, and a rock beside it, and a smooth-pointed drinking-horn on it, and a beautiful fresh well at its foot; and there was a great drouth on Diarmuid after the sea-journey, and he had a mind to drink a hornful of the water. But when he stooped to it he heard a great noise coming towards him, and he knew then there was enchantment in the water. "I will drink my fill of it for all that." And a Man of Enchantments came towards him armed: "It is no right thing to be walking through my thickets and to be drinking up my share of water." They fought till the end of the day, and the Enchanter made a leap into the bottom of the well; and in the evening, when the Enchanter was making his leap into the well again, Diarmuid threw his arms about his neck, thinking to stop him, but it is what happened, he fell in himself.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Diarmuid went following after the Enchanter, and found before him a beautiful wide flowery plain, and a comely royal city in the plain; and when they saw him following after the Enchanter, they shut the gates, and the whole army turned on Diarmuid. But that put no fear on him, and he went through them and over them like a hawk would go through little birds, killing all before him; and Diarmuid, all full of hurts and wounds after the hard fight, lay down on the plain. A very strong daring champion came then and kicked at him: "It is not to do you any hurt or harm I am come, but to say to you it is a bad sleeping-place for you to have, and it on your ill-wisher's lawn." Diarmuid followed him a long, long way, till they came to a high-topped city, and there was a good welcome before him for his own sake and the sake of his people, and he was put in a house of healing, and good herbs were put to his hurts till he was smooth and sound again. Three days and three nights Diarmuid stopped in that city, and the best feast he ever found was given to him all through; and the champion told him it was Land-Under-Wave, and that the man that had fought with him was its king.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn Routs the High King of Greece

region.en: Land of Sorcha, western ocean (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 索爾卡之國，西海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: Following Diarmuid's trail of meat-leavings, Finn is hosted by the King of Sorcha — himself once Finn's hired man — when the High King of Greece comes to put the whole world under him. Finn takes the protection of the country on himself, and with Osgar and Oisin and Goll makes such slaughter of the Greeks' champions that the King of Greece carries home what is left of his people, swearing to banish the Sons of the Gael to the ends of the earth.
summary.zh: 循迪爾穆德留下的肉屑而行，芬恩受「曾受雇於芬恩」的索爾卡王款待；此時希臘至高王正欲將全世界納入其轄下。芬恩立誓護國，與奧斯加、歐辛、戈爾將希臘勇士屠戮殆盡，希臘王攜殘部歸國，發誓要將蓋爾之子放逐至地極。

sensitivity.note: Finn's sea-expedition to protect a king who had served him years before turns employer-retainer law (wages never refused) into transmarine heroism; the Greek high-king parallels Daire Donn of the White Strand. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: Now, as to Finn and his people, when they thought Diarmuid was too long away from them, they made ladders of the cords of the ship and put them against the rock, looking for him, and after a while they found the leavings of the meat he had eaten, for Diarmuid never ate meat without leaving some after him. Finn looked then on every side, and he saw a rider coming towards him over the plain on a dark-coloured beautiful horse, having a bridle of red gold; and they went on till they came to a wide, large dwelling-place full of arms, and a great troop of armed men on the green before the fort. At the end of that time Finn asked what country was he in, and the man that brought him there told him it was the land of Sorcha, and that he himself was its king — "And I was with yourself one time, Finn, son of Cumhal, taking your wages through the length of a year in Ireland."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn and the King of Sorcha called a great gathering of the people, and while it was going on they saw a woman-messenger coming through the crowd: "The whole of the bay and the harbour is full of ships and of boats, and there are armies all through the country robbing all before them." "I know well, it is the High King of Greece is in it, for he has a mind to put the entire world under him, and to get hold of this country like every other." The King of Sorcha looked at Finn, and Finn understood it was help from him he was asking, and it is what he said: "I take the protection of this country on myself so long as I am in it." He and his people rose up, and the King of Sorcha along with them, and when they came up with the strange army they made great slaughter of its champions, and those they did not kill made no better stand than a flock of frightened birds, till there were hardly enough of them left to tell the story. And at the last the King of Greece brought all his people back home, the way no more of them would be put an end to.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: And then Finn and the King of Sorcha called another great gathering, and while it was going on, they saw coming towards them a great troop of champions, bearing flags of many-coloured silk, and grey swords at their sides and high spears reared up over their heads, and in the front of them was Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne. And it would take too long to tell how Finn made the Hard Servant bring home his fifteen men that he had brought away; and when he had brought them back to Ireland, the whole of the Fianna were watching to see him ride away again, himself and his long-legged horse. But while they were watching him, he vanished from them, and all they could see was a mist, and it stretching out towards the sea. And that is the story of the Hard Servant, and of Diarmuid's adventures on the island Under-Wave.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Miodac's Riddles and the House of the Quicken Trees
title.zh: 米奧達克之謎與花楸樹之屋

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VI, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Miodac, son of the King of Lochlann, passes himself off as a poet and tests Finn with verses: an army riding to victory with no horses but plants and branches — bees, says Finn; a woman swifter than any horse — the River Boinn, whose going never stops. Having found Finn out as a reader, he bids the Fianna into his House of the Quicken Trees: colour-fading walls, one door shut, a stenching fire, an enchantment that holds them to the floor — until Diarmuid makes an end of Miodac and the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods and takes the spell off the floor with their blood.
summary.zh: 洛赫蘭王之子米奧達克假扮詩人，以謎語試探芬恩：一支騎向勝利的軍隊卻無馬騎，只有草木枝葉——芬恩答曰蜂群；一位賽過駿馬的女子——芬恩答曰永不停止奔流的博因河。試出芬恩善解後，他將菲亞納誘入花楸樹之屋：彩壁褪色、七門僅存一閉門、香火轉惡臭、咒術使人黏地——直到迪爾穆德誅米奧達克與洪流群島三王，以其血破除地板咒術。

sensitivity.note: The riddle-contest (focusing Finn's wisdom) is the standard prelude to the enchanted-hostel trap; 'Quicken' = rowan, whose blood-breaking of enchantment echoes the rowan's protective uses in Gaelic belief. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was by treachery Miodac brought them in, giving himself out to be a poet, and making poems for Finn to make out the meaning of. A verse he made about a great army that he saw riding over the plains to victory, and robbing all before it, and the riders of it having no horses but plants and branches. "I understand that, it was an army of bees you saw, that was gathering riches from the flowers as it went." And another verse Miodac made was about a woman in Ireland that was swifter than the swiftest horse. "I know that; that woman is the River Boinn; and if she goes slow itself, she is swifter in the end than the swiftest horse, for her going never stops." And other verses he made about Angus' house at Brugh na Boinn, but Finn made them all out.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And after that he said he had a feast ready for them, and he bade them go into his House of the Quicken Trees till he would bring it; and it was a beautiful house, having walls of every colour, and foreign coverings of every colour on the floor, and a fire that gave out a very pleasant smoke.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after a while Finn said: "It is a wonder such a beautiful house to be here." "There is a greater wonder than that; that fire that was so pleasant when we came in is giving out now the worst stench in the world." "There is a greater wonder than that; the walls that were of all colours are now but rough boards joined together." "There is a greater wonder than that; where there were seven high doors to the house there is now but one little door, and it shut." "Indeed, there is a more wonderful thing than that, for we sat down on beautiful coverings, and now there is nothing between us and the bare ground, and it as cold as the snow of one night." And he tried to rise up, but he could not stir, or any of the rest of them, for there was enchantment that kept them where they were; and it was the treachery of Miodac, and the spells of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods, that had brought them into that danger.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: And at the last it was Diarmuid that made an end of Miodac that was so treacherous, and of the Three Kings of the Island of the Floods, and took the enchantment off the floor of the House of the Rowan Trees with their blood.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VI, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: Grania Answers Finn at the Wedding of Tara
title.zh: 格拉尼亞在塔拉婚宴上妙答芬恩

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book VII, ch. I, eBook #14465

summary.en: Betrothed to grey-haired Finn at Tara, Grania is put to the riddles of a man quick with questions and better with answers: whiter than snow — the truth; hotter than fire — a hospitable man's face when a stranger comes and the house is empty; sharper than a sword — the wit of a woman between two men; quicker than the wind — a woman's mind. She has no liking for Finn, and when the cap falls from Diarmuid's love-spot at the dogs' feast, her blood rises against the bridegroom forever.
summary.zh: 塔拉婚約既成，善問的芬恩以謎語相試，而格拉尼亞的回答更勝一籌：比雪更白——真理；比火更熱——客至而家空時好客之人的面容；比劍更利——兩男之間的女子之智；比風更疾——女子之心。她本無意於芬恩；群犬宴上迪爾穆德的帽子滑落、露出愛斑之際，她的心便永遠背離了新郎。

sensitivity.note: Grania's riddle-duel is a wisdom-contest embedded in the betrothal scene and quoted through the whole pursuit; the falling cap revealing the love-spot is the love-charm mechanism of the Diarmuid cycle. Tara pin, as the wedding was held at the seat of the High King.

passages.text: Finn gathered together the seven battalions of the Fianna to Teamhair, and when Grania saw grey-haired Finn she said: "It is a great wonder it was not for Oisin Finn asked me, for he would be more fitting for me than a man that is older than my father." But they talked together for a while, and Finn was putting questions to Grania, for she had the name of being very quick with answers. "What is whiter than snow?" "The truth." "What is the best colour?" "The colour of childhood." "What is hotter than fire?" "The face of a hospitable man when he sees a stranger coming in, and the house empty." "What has a taste more bitter than poison?" "The reproach of an enemy." "What is best for a champion?" "His doings to be high, and his pride to be low." "What is the best of jewels?" "A knife." "What is sharper than a sword?" "The wit of a woman between two men." "What is quicker than the wind?" "A woman's mind," said Grania. And indeed she was telling no lie when she said that.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the wedding-feast in the king's feasting-house, a Druid of Finn's people named the champions for her at her asking — Goll the ready fighter, Osgar son of Oisin, thin-legged Caoilte, proud Lugaidh's Son — and then: "Who is that sweet-worded man with the dark hair, and cheeks like the rowan berry, on the left side of Oisin, son of Finn?" "That is Diarmuid, grandson of Duibhne, that is the best lover of women in the whole world." And after the feast had gone on a while, their own feast was made for the dogs outside; and Diarmuid was used to keep his cap always over the love-spot the woman had left on his forehead, and it chanced, while he was driving the dogs apart, the cap fell from him, and Grania was looking at him as it fell, and great love for him came on her there and then.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.

passages.text: She filled the great golden cup with wine that had enchantment in it, and all that drank of it fell into a heavy sleep — Finn and the king and the whole company, but only Oisin and Osgar and Caoilte and Diarmuid and Diorraing; and when they were all in their sleep, Grania rose up softly, and turned her face to Diarmuid: "Will you take my love, Diarmuid, son of Duibhne, and will you bring me away out of this house to-night?"
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book VII, ch. I; not verbatim.
